c.tagline: The 'dawn of happiness,' Thailand's first capital, now a UNESCO park of lotus-ringed temple ruins

card: Accepted at larger hotels; cash preferred at markets and small guesthouses
rides: bicycle rental (popular within the historical park)

taxi.fareNote: Renting a bicycle is the classic way to explore Sukhothai Historical Park's flat, spread-out ruins

emergency.note: Tourist police (1155) can assist with English-language support

walk: The historical park is spread out but flat and best explored by rented bicycle; New Sukhothai town itself is walkable for its market and guesthouses

safety.safety: Very safe, low-key destination popular with independent travelers
safety.crime: Very low crime; standard bicycle and heat precautions apply within the park

hood_landmark.New Sukhothai (Town): New Sukhothai's night market and guesthouse strip
hood_landmark.Wat Si Chum: Wat Si Chum's giant seated Buddha peering through a narrow gap
hood_landmark.Ramkhamhaeng National Museum: The Ramkhamhaeng National Museum's Sukhothai artifacts
hood_landmark.Si Satchanalai (day-trip): Si Satchanalai Historical Park's quieter riverside ruins

avoid.reason: Watch for stray dogs when cycling the Historical Park at dawn or dusk; otherwise nothing specific — usual awareness.

hood_desc: The modern town about 12km from the ruins, with most guesthouses, restaurants, and the night market.
The heart of the UNESCO-listed historical park, with the iconic lotus-bud chedi of Wat Mahathat and the largest concentration of ruins.
A separate temple complex just outside the central zone, famous for its enormous seated Buddha statue.
A small museum near the park entrance providing context on the Sukhothai Kingdom's art and history.
A quieter, less-visited sister historical park about an hour away, with riverside ruins and fewer crowds.

water.note: Drink bottled water; tap water is not potable.

transit.sys: Songthaews between New Sukhothai and the historical park; bicycle rental within the park
transit.map: Not centrally published; songthaews run regularly between town and the park
transit.note: Bicycle rental at the park entrance is the classic, recommended way to see the ruins

transport.air: Sukhothai Airport (THS), about 30 min from New Sukhothai, with flights from Bangkok and Chiang Mai
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Sukhothai
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect to Bangkok (about 6-7 hr) and Chiang Mai (about 5 hr)
transport.car: Rental cars available; well connected via Highway 12

net.m: Moderate 4G coverage in town and the historical park
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels
net.ap: An AIS or DTAC tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: Not obligatory but appreciated for guides

food.name: Kuay tiao Sukhothai
food.desc: Thin rice noodles in clear pork broth with roast pork, green beans, peanuts, dried chilli and palm sugar - the town's own noodle bowl.

places.name: Jay Hae
places.note: Family roadside shop famous nationwide; broth from pork bones only, no stock powder. Open 8am to 4pm.

places.name: Ta Pui Noodles
places.area: Muang Kao, near the Old City
places.note: Long-running local noodle house closer to the ruins, a favourite pre-cycling breakfast.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.area: New Sukhothai, near the clock tower
places.note: Several noodle carts serve the local recipe late into the evening.

food.name: Pla pao (salt-crusted grilled fish)
food.desc: Whole Yom River fish packed in salt and lemongrass, grilled over charcoal and eaten with fiery seafood dipping sauce and herbs.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Charcoal grills line the market; point at the fish you want and it is cooked to order.

places.name: Poo Restaurant
places.note: Traveller-friendly kitchen with grilled fish, Thai standards and an unusually good drinks list.

places.name: Riverside food stalls, Yom River
places.note: Evening stalls by the bridge grill river fish and serve it with sticky rice.

food.name: Khanom jeen
food.desc: Soft fermented rice noodles doused in curry or fish-based sauce and piled with raw vegetables and herbs - a northern breakfast habit.

places.name: Talat Sot morning market
places.note: Best before 9am; vendors ladle several curries over the noodles for a few baht.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Evening version with a choice of nam ya and nam ngiao sauces.

places.name: Ta Pui Noodles
places.note: Noodle shop near the historical park with the regional rice-noodle repertoire.

food.name: Som tam and gai yang
food.desc: Pounded green papaya salad with lime, chilli and fish sauce, eaten with charcoal-grilled marinated chicken and sticky rice.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Papaya-salad pounders and chicken grills side by side; order the sticky rice with it.

places.name: Poo Restaurant
places.note: Milder versions for visitors, with cold beer and English menus.

places.name: Food stalls at the Old City gates
places.note: Handy lunch between temples, with grilled chicken and salads under the trees.

food.name: Khanom wan (Thai sweets)
food.desc: Coconut-and-palm-sugar sweets - khanom krok pancakes, sticky rice parcels, jellies and mango sticky rice - sold by the tray at markets.

places.name: Talat Sot morning market
places.note: The widest range of home-made sweets, mostly gone by mid-morning.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Coconut pancakes cooked in dimpled pans while you watch.

places.name: Dream Cafe
places.note: Antique-crammed cafe and restaurant, a long-standing spot for Thai desserts and coffee.

food.name: Khao moo daeng
food.desc: Sliced red-roast pork over rice with a sweet gravy, cucumber and a boiled egg - the classic quick Thai lunch plate.

places.name: Jay Hae
places.note: Roasts its own pork for the noodles, so the rice plates are just as good.

places.name: Talat Sot morning market
places.note: Rice-and-pork counters open from early morning, cheap and fast.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Several stalls hang the glazed pork out front; easy to point and order.

food.name: Cha yen (Thai iced tea)
food.desc: Strong orange-hued tea sweetened with condensed milk and poured over ice - the standard antidote to Sukhothai's heat.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Drink carts everywhere, made to order in a plastic bag or cup.

places.name: Dream Cafe
places.note: Relaxed, atmospheric room for iced tea, coffee and herbal drinks.

places.name: Cafes by the historical park
places.note: Cluster of small cafes at the park entrance selling iced tea and coffee to cyclists.

food.name: Cold Thai beer
food.desc: Light lagers such as Singha, Chang and Leo, poured over ice - what Thais drink with grilled fish and spicy salads.

places.name: Poo Restaurant
places.note: Best-known bar-restaurant in town for beer, with imports as well as Thai lagers.

places.name: Chopper Bar
places.note: Two-storey traveller bar with live music most nights and a street-view terrace.

places.name: Sukhothai night market
places.note: Buy a bottle with your grilled fish and drink at the shared tables.

landmarks: Wat Mahathat (Sukhothai Historical Park)
The spiritual centrepiece of Thailand's first capital, a vast UNESCO-listed temple of lotus-bud stupas and serene seated Buddhas among reflecting ponds.
Wat Si Chum
Home of the awe-inspiring Phra Achana, a 15-metre seated Buddha whose gold-leafed fingers peek through a narrow slit in its mondop walls.
Wat Sa Si
A graceful island temple set in a lotus pond, its Sri Lankan-style bell stupa and walking Buddha silhouette defining Sukhothai sunsets.
Wat Si Sawai
A former Khmer-Hindu shrine with three magnificent corn-cob prangs, later converted into a Buddhist temple, ringed by peaceful lawns and ponds.
Wat Phra Phai Luang
A sprawling 12th-century Khmer-era complex north of the walls, believed to be the original centre of Sukhothai before the kingdom's rise.
Wat Saphan Hin
A hilltop temple reached by an ancient slate pathway, where a 12.5-metre standing Buddha has surveyed the plains for seven centuries.
Ramkhamhaeng National Museum
The essential primer on Sukhothai civilisation, displaying masterpieces of Thailand's most graceful Buddha style alongside a replica of the famous inscription stone.
Wat Chang Lom
A Sri Lankan-style bell stupa carried by a ring of 36 sculpted brick-and-stucco elephants, east of the old city walls.
Wat Traphang Thong
A living monastery on a golden lotus pond entered by a wooden footbridge, sheltering a revered Buddha footprint from the 14th century.
Si Satchanalai Historical Park
Sukhothai's UNESCO sister city an hour north, where jungle-fringed ruins like elephant-ringed Wat Chang Lom feel gloriously crowd-free.

train.note: Sukhothai has no station. The nearest railhead is Phitsanulok, about an hour east by bus, on the State Railway of Thailand northern line (https://www.dticket.railway.co.th/) with trains to Bangkok in around 6 hours and Chiang Mai in 6. Sawankhalok has a small branch-line station with a limited service. Most visitors take the bus or fly into Sukhothai's private airport.

bus.note: No international coaches. Sukhothai's terminal is on the edge of New Sukhothai, with Win Tour and Transport Co. (https://www.transport.co.th/) services to Bangkok in about 6-7 hours, Chiang Mai (5-6) and frequent local buses to Phitsanulok. Book through 12Go (https://12go.asia/). Songthaews shuttle between New Sukhothai and the historical park, 12 km west.

ferry.note: Sukhothai is inland in the northern plains with no navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Phitsanulok
half.blurb: Riverside city home to a revered bronze Buddha image enshrined at Wat Phra Si Rattana Mahathat.

half.name: Kamphaeng Phet Historical Park
half.blurb: Ruined former fortress city with brick temple remains from the Sukhothai and Ayutthaya periods.

half.name: Ramkhamhaeng National Park
half.blurb: Forested mountain park with waterfalls, caves, and hiking trails above the old Sukhothai plain.
